> When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew to Lake Manasa, while one-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a grove of land-lotuses. O maiden, you see three pairs of swans playing with delight in the water adorned with young lotus stalks; tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

**Syntactical Arrangement:** O maiden! When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of the flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth flew from the water's edge to the grove of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen playing with delight in the water adorned with young lotus stalks. Then, tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

**Meaning:** O beloved one, sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. When the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of the group went to Lake Manasa, one-eighth of them flew from the edge of the water to the grove of land-lotuses, and three pairs of swans were seen playing with great affection in the water, which was beautiful with soft lotus stalks. Then, say, how many swans were in that group? (3)

**Calculation:** Square root factor 10, one-eighth <gloss>1/8</gloss>, visible <gloss>6</gloss>. Since the rule stated is to subtract the fractional parts, here, by dividing the visible amount <gloss>6</gloss> by the remainder of the parts <gloss>7/8</gloss>, the resulting visible amount is <gloss>48/7</gloss>, and the square root factor is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of the factor is <gloss>40/7</gloss>; squaring this gives <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Added to this is <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Added to half the factor <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squared, the total number of swans is 144.

**Elaboration:** According to the rule stated in the previous verse, when one-eighth <gloss>1/8</gloss> is subtracted from one <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss>, it becomes <gloss>7/8</gloss>. When the visible amount 6 is divided by this, <gloss>6/1 divided by 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7</gloss>. Upon converting the seven, 48/7 becomes the visible quantity. Similarly, when the square root factor 10 is divided by 7/8, <gloss>10/1 divided by 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7</gloss>. Upon converting the seven, 80/7 becomes the root quantity. Now, taking 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the root factor, perform the operation according to the method stated in the verse above. That is, half of the root factor is 40/7. Squaring this gives 1600/49. To this, the visible quantity 48/7 is...

<summary>This page provides a mathematical problem concerning a flock of swans, involving square roots and fractional parts, followed by a detailed calculation and elaboration to determine the total number of swans.</summary>

Vasudeva is the supreme Brahman. His manifestation is the supreme Person <note>original: "Purusha"</note>; He is unmanifest, devoid of qualities <note>original: "nirguna"</note>, tranquil, beyond the twenty-five principles <note>original: "tattvas"</note>, and immutable, meaning He is without change. 12.

->The god, abiding within nature, pervades everything both inside and out.<-
->Sankarshana, at the beginning of creation, created the waters and deposited his seed within them. 13.<-

The author explains that since it is impossible for the pure Brahman to be the cause of the world, he says: "Abiding within nature," meaning qualified by <term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>, and "pervading everything inside and out," because He is the material cause of the world. All these attributes are to be understood as belonging to Sankarshana, who is a portion of Vasudeva, by realizing his identity with Vasudeva. Sankarshana, who is a portion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he deposited his "seed," a specific power. 13.

The god Sankarshana, who is everywhere perceptible, entered into this very nature and first created the waters. Afterward, he placed his own energy in the form of a seed into that water. 13.

->That egg became golden and was covered in darkness on all sides.<-
->There, Aniruddha, the eternal one, became manifest first. 14.<-

The author now explains what happened next. That water, combined with his energy, became a golden, spherical egg, covered everywhere by darkness both inside and out. The meaning is that a golden egg was born in the space filled with darkness. In that golden egg, Aniruddha, the eternal one—who is Sankarshana, a portion of Vasudeva—became manifest first. He was not born, as the doctrine of pre-existing effects is accepted. Just as oil exists in sesame seeds and is merely manifested, not created. 14.

That energy in the form of a seed took the shape of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There (inside the egg), the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. 14.

->This Lord is recited in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha.<-
->He is indeed called Aditya because he was the first being, and because of his expansion, he is called Surya. 15.<-

Now, for the better understanding of the people, the author provides his other names. This Lord Aniruddha, who is a portion of Sankarshana and endowed with the six qualities of divine majesty <note>original: "shaidgunya-aishvarya"</note>, is recited or described in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha because he dwells inside the golden egg. The meaning is that his other well-known name in the Vedas is Hiranyagarbha. He is indeed called Aditya because he was the first to be manifested. Because he expanded to create this world, he is called Surya.

"Hiranyagarbha existed in the beginning; he was the sole lord of all created beings."

This is the scriptural testimony. 15.

This very Lord is Hiranyagarbha, who is mentioned in the Vedas. At first...

<summary>This page explains the Vedantic creation narrative within the Surya Siddhanta, detailing the manifestation of the supreme Brahman into Sankarshana and the subsequent emergence of the golden egg, Hiranyagarbha, and Aniruddha.</summary>
<keywords>Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Aniruddha, Hiranyagarbha, creation, golden egg, Surya, Vedas, Brahman</keywords>

A wise man, knowing his own limitations, should not proposition a woman who is suspicious, guarded, afraid, or under the supervision of a mother-in-law. || 27 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, on the causes of acquaintance and the methods of approach, in the fifth book, on the wives of others, of the Kamasutram by Vatsyayana.

"Suspicious" means one who has doubts about the suitor. "Guarded" means protected by her attendants. "Afraid" means fearful of her husband. "Under the supervision of a mother-in-law" means staying under the authority of the mother-in-law. "Should not proposition" means should not desire. "Knowing his own limitations" means arriving at the firm realization that "I am incapable in this situation." || 27 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth section, on approaches.

Thus ends the second chapter, on the causes of acquaintance and the methods of approach, in the fifth book, on the wives of others, of the Jayamangala commentary on the Kamasutram, written by Yashodhara.

Chapter 3.

Even when an approach is made, women who are steady, bold, and worth testing should not be approached if their intentions are not revealed; therefore, the examination of sentiments is described—
One who is making an approach should examine the woman’s inclinations; by that, her sentiments become tested. || 1 ||

Just as one approaches a maiden, one should examine her inclinations, meaning her behavior. Indeed, by this indirect examination, her sentiments are tested. || 1 ||

He explains how she should be won over—
One should win over a woman who does not reveal her secret thoughts through a female messenger. || 2 ||

"Who does not reveal her secret thoughts" means one who does not make her amorous feelings known. One should win her over through a female messenger because of the messenger's boldness. || 2 ||

One should recognize as having a divided mind a woman who, having rejected an approach, later engages in contact again; one should win her over gradually. || 3 ||

"Having rejected an approach" means after refusing the overture made by the hero. "Later engages in contact again" means after some days have passed, she enters into contact with the hero. "One should recognize as having a divided mind" means she is to be examined, thinking, "What should I do? I do not know." One should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. || 3 ||

Regarding this, he mentions a specific detail—
If she is seen again wearing special ornaments after having rejected an approach, one should approach her in that same manner and

"It must be given. Its outcome depends upon him," and "Therefore, you take it away." Hearing this, as soon as he awoke and searched for the gold knot, he saw it was empty and thought, "Alas! How has the wealth I earned with such difficulty been lost so easily? How shall I, now penniless, show my face to my wife or my friends?" Having decided this, he went back to Vardhamanapura. There, having earned five hundred gold coins in just one year, he set out for his home again by a different route.

As the sun was setting, he arrived at that same banyan tree. "Woe, alas, woe! What has this wretch of a fate begun?" he thought. "The same demon in the form of the banyan tree has appeared again." Thinking this, while pretending to be asleep, he saw those same two men on its branch. One of them said, "Worker, why did you give this Somilaka five hundred gold coins? Do you not know that he has nothing beyond food and clothing?" The other replied, "Oh, Worker, I must give to those who are industrious. The outcome is up to them. Why do you blame me?" Hearing this, Somilaka searched for the knot, and seeing that it was empty, he was filled with supreme detachment and thought, "Alas! What is the use of living without wealth? I shall hang myself from this banyan tree and give up my life."

Having decided this, he made a rope of sacred grass, fastened a noose around his neck, approached a branch, and just as he was about to cast himself off after tying it, a man in the sky said this: "Oh Somilaka, do not act so rashly. I am that same wealth-taker, who takes away your wealth that exceeds your food and clothing

<summary>Somilaka the weaver is repeatedly robbed of his wealth by a demon, leading him to attempt suicide at a banyan tree, where he hears the demon justify his actions as a response to the weaver's lack of true necessity.</summary>

If war has indeed arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? For, who is that servant or minister who, without careful consideration, advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own post at the very start? Furthermore, one should always endeavor to conquer enemies through means other than war, as the outcome of a struggle between two combatants is never certain. Moreover, one should attempt to subdue the enemy by using diplomacy, bribery, sowing dissension, or all three combined, but never by war alone. Additionally, everyone considers themselves brave when they have not yet encountered the conflict, for who would not be proud when they have not yet seen the power of the enemy? Furthermore, one does not stir up such terrible strife among creatures, as success is rarely achieved through minor means and the fruits of war are never great. Therefore, seeing that war has arrived, let it be disregarded. For:

The <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>the ruddy sheldrake, acting as a counselor in this fable</gloss> says, "O King, war is not to be pursued. For what kind of servant or minister is it who advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own station without first deliberating? Furthermore, one should endeavor to conquer an opponent by means of conciliation and other strategies, but never by armed conflict, since it is impossible to know for certain which of the two combatants will emerge victorious. Moreover, one should attempt to resolve matters with an enemy by using conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension, either individually or together, but never by fighting. Besides, every person is a hero as long as they have not yet faced a battle, for who would not be arrogant without having seen the strength of another?"

<summary>This page contains a debate on political strategy, arguing against immediate war in favor of diplomatic measures like conciliation and bribery.</summary>
<keywords>Hitopadesha, diplomacy, war, statecraft, Chakravaka, conflict resolution</keywords>

Oulong’an had once stored a case of cups and bowls separately, with the velvet covers undisturbed, yet the vessels had all vanished. He spoke wildly and unpredictably. Liu laughed and said, "One by one, do not question it further."

**Jiaona**

Scholar Kong, of the Snow Hat clan <note>original: "雪笠", likely referring to the lineage of Confucius</note>, was a descendant of the Sage. He was a person of reserve and skilled at poetry. He had a close friend living in Tiantai who sent a letter inviting him over. Kong went to visit, but as it happened, his friend had passed away. Destitute and unable to return home, he resided in Putuo Temple, working for the monks as a copyist. About a hundred paces west of the temple stood the residence of Mr. Shan. The master was a former nobleman who had fallen into poverty due to a great lawsuit. His family members were few, and they had moved away to live in the countryside, leaving the house vacant. One day, as heavy snow fell and the world was silent with no travelers, Kong happened to pass by the gate. A youth emerged with a truly elegant appearance. Seeing Kong, he hurried forward to greet him with the proper rites, offering his condolences and immediately inviting him inside. Kong was pleased and readily followed him in. The house was not very large, but everywhere hung brocade curtains. On the walls were many paintings and calligraphy by the ancients. On the desk lay a book with a label that read *Trifles from the Langhuan Library* <note>original: "瑯環瑣", a reference to a mythical celestial library</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the story of Scholar Kong, a refined descendant of Confucius who, while stranded in Tiantai, encounters a mysterious and elegant youth residing in a supposedly vacant mansion.</summary>
<keywords>Scholar Kong, Jiaona, Putuo Temple, Mr. Shan, Langhuan Library, reserve</keywords>

<meta>Continues from Volume 3, page 6. The protagonist, Cheng, has returned from captivity and is feuding with his brothers over inheritance and property.</meta>

They all went out to the fields and houses, and once the estate was settled, the brothers became angry that he had bought favor. They went to his gate to humiliate and harass him. Cheng had been among bandits for a long time and had grown accustomed to ferocity. Upon hearing this, he became furious and said, "Now that I have returned, no one is willing to provide me with a single room. Fortunately, my third younger brother remembered our blood ties, yet you even reproach him for this? Are you trying to drive me away?" He threw stones at Xiao. Xiao, Ren, and Yi each brought out their staffs and, taking Zhong and Xin along, beat him countless times. Cheng did not wait for them to sue him; he sued them to the magistrate first. The magistrate then sent someone to invite Youyu to testify. Youyu could not help but come. When asked, he bowed his head in shame and remained silent, only shedding tears. The magistrate pressed him for an answer, and he only requested that the official judge the matter. The magistrate then ordered Xiao and the others to each contribute a portion of their land and property to return to Cheng, making the seven shares equal. From this point on, Ren, Yi, and Cheng grew increasingly affectionate and respectful toward one another. During a conversation, the subject of their mother's burial suddenly came up, and they all wept. Cheng stated, "To be this unfilial is to be a beast." He then intended to open the grave and rebury her. Ren and Yi rushed to tell Youyu, who hurried home to remonstrate and stop him. Cheng did not listen and set a date for the act.

<summary>Cheng returns from captivity to find his brothers hostile regarding family inheritance. After a physical confrontation and legal intervention, the brothers reconcile, though Cheng insists on reburying their mother to honor her properly.</summary>
<keywords>inheritance dispute, familial reconciliation, filial piety, legal judgment, reburial</keywords>

[They] used boards and sticks on me, and I just stood there. I don't know what they used, but they beat me once, and my face was broken in two places. We heard that the Mistress <note>referring to Aunt Xue</note> has a type of medicine here for treating wounds from beatings. Could you, Miss, find a pill for me?

Baochai heard this and hurriedly ordered Ying'er to find two pills for Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, you go and send my greetings on my behalf; I will not go." Ping'er promised Baochai and left. This is left aside for now.

As for Xiangling, after she had seen the others and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the rest went to the mother's place, and she went to the Xiaoxiang Pavilion. By this time, Daiyu was already more than half recovered. Seeing Xiangling had also moved into the Garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling laughed and said, "Now that I have finally moved in and have some free time, it would be my great fortune if you would teach me how to write poetry." Daiyu laughed and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly teach you the basics." Xiangling laughed and said, "If that is really so, I will take you as my teacher. You must not get tired of it." Daiyu said, "What is difficult about it? It is nothing more than the <term>qichengzhuanhe</term> <gloss>the four-part structure of a poem: opening, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. In the middle, the development and transition are two pairs of couplets: flat tones must be paired with oblique tones; abstract concepts must be paired with concrete ones, and concrete ones with abstract. If you truly have an extraordinary line, it is acceptable even if the flat/oblique tones and the abstract/concrete pairs do not match."

Xiangling laughed and said, "No wonder when I often take an old poetry book and secretly read a few poems, there are some that are perfectly matched and others that are not. I have also heard it said that, 'the first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, while the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this, and some have errors in the second, fourth, and sixth characters. That is why I have been puzzled every day. Now that I hear you speak, it turns out that these rules are actually of little consequence; it is only important that the words and phrases are fresh and novel." Daiyu said, "That is precisely the point. The words and phrases are ultimately secondary matters; the most important thing is establishing the intent. If the sentiment and interest are genuine, even if the words and phrases are not polished, it is naturally good. This is what is called 'not letting the words harm the intent'."

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>Lu You, a famous Song dynasty poet</note> lines, 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, the scent remains for long; the ancient inkstone is slightly worn, the gathered ink is thick,' they are truly vivid and interesting!" Daiyu said, "Because you do not know poetry, you love these shallow and accessible ones. Once you enter this pattern, you will never learn anything else. Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Collection of Wang Mojie* <note>Wang Wei, a Tang dynasty poet</note> here. You should first ponder his one hundred five-character regulated verses carefully until you know them thoroughly. Then, read one hundred twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character regulated verses. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>Li Bai, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your belly, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, and Bao. Since you are such an extremely clever and sharp person, you won't need a year of effort before you become a true poetess!" Xiangling heard this and laughed, "If that is the case, good Miss, take the book out for me, and I will take it back. It will be good to recite a few poems at night." When Daiyu heard this, she ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Youcheng's <note>Another name for Wang Wei</note> five-character regulated verses and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones with red circles; they are all selected by me. Read one poem after another. If there is something you don't understand, ask your maid, or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Hengwu Courtyard. Ignoring all other matters, she sat under the lamp and read them one by one. Although Baochai urged her several times to sleep, she would not. Seeing her such painstaking effort, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, after Daiyu had just finished washing and combing, she saw Xiangling humming as she delivered the book, wanting to trade it for Du's regulated verses. Daiyu laughed and asked, "How many have you memorized in total?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have read all the ones marked with red circles." Daiyu said, "Have you grasped some of them?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have grasped some, but I don't know if I'm right. Let me recite them to you and see."

<summary>Daiyu instructs Xiangling on the principles of composing poetry and assigns her a course of study based on classic Tang dynasty poets.</summary>
<keywords>Daiyu, Xiangling, Baochai, Poetry, Tang Dynasty, Literary study</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to appoint famous scholars to win popular support. Following this, he recommended Cai Yong for his talent, and Dong Zhuo ordered that he be summoned.</meta>

Cai Yong did not comply at first. Dong Zhuo was furious and sent a messenger to tell him, "If you do not come, I will wipe out your clan." Terrified, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Dong Zhuo was overjoyed to see him and promoted him three times in a single month, eventually appointing him as a Palace Attendant <note>original: 侍中</note>, treating him with great intimacy and favor. <gloss>He always relied on the patronage of Wang Feng and Yang Xiong; he would end his life as firewood and be buried by the woodcutters of Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Young Emperor <note>original: 少帝</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were trapped in the Yong'an Palace, with clothing and food becoming increasingly scarce. The Young Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>As the former king once said, the sun and moon in this place feel endless.</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds dance and fly; in this cold palace and abandoned temple, I am alone, and my years are my own.</gloss> The poem read:

The tender grass is green, congealed in mist,
The pair of swallows flutter and fly.
The Luo River is a blue stream,
Envied by those upon the road.
<gloss>The first half of the poem describes the swallows and looks into the distance.</gloss>
Deep within the azure clouds lies my former palace,
<gloss>Gazing at the old palace, unable to fly, truly not as fortunate as the pair of swallows returning to their old nest. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will wield loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the grievances in my heart?
<gloss>The second half is an expression of his personal wishes. A fine poem.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo often sent people to eavesdrop. That day, they intercepted this poem and presented it to him. Dong Zhuo said, "He is full of resentment and writes poems. I have a valid reason to kill him." <gloss>Killing him provides a famous justification, setting an example for the world.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to take eighteen armed men into the palace to murder the Emperor. The Emperor and the Empress were on the upper floor when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was terrified. Li Ru presented the Emperor with a cup of poisoned wine. <gloss>Suggesting that such a poem deserves this wine, which is the most elegant way to end him.</gloss>

<summary>Cai Yong is forced into service by Dong Zhuo, while the imprisoned Young Emperor expresses his despair through a poem, leading Dong Zhuo to plot his execution.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, Consort Tang, Poisoned Wine</keywords>

### Nineteenth Chapter 19.

Now we shall explain the chapter regarding the care of the wounded <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>rules for the care of the wounded</gloss>.

Here begins the explanation of the <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>chapter on the regimen for the wounded</gloss>.

First, seek a suitable dwelling for the wounded patient; that dwelling should be constructed in an auspicious location. 1. In a house with a favorable site, clean, free from wind and sun, and protected from drafts, there will be no physical, traumatic, or mental diseases. 2. In that place, provide a bed that is uncrowded, well-spread, pleasant, with the head facing east, and accompanied by weapons <note>often for protection or religious warding</note>. 3. The wounded patient will have ease of movement and comfort on a well-spread bed. The gods dwell in the eastern direction, therefore the head should not be placed toward the east. 4.

<note>(Verse 42) connected with the bandage.</note>

Consume lentils <term>māṣa</term> <gloss>black gram</gloss>, sprouted, purified, and sweet, prepared with cold fruits and cooked in buffalo meat broth with yogurt and pomegranate. When seasoned with <term>āmalakī</term> <gloss>Emblica officinalis</gloss>, coriander, cumin, and dry ginger, and consumed with food, this broth prevents the depletion of <term>śukra</term> <gloss>semen/reproductive vitality</gloss>. 8
> Thus ends the buffalo meat aphrodisiac broth.

One who eats fresh fish or fried <term>śapharī</term> <gloss>small cyprinid fish</gloss> in hot clarified butter <term>ghṛta</term> will not suffer exhaustion during sexual intercourse. 9
> Thus ends the fish fried in clarified butter for aphrodisiac purposes.

One seeking offspring should consume <term>rohitā</term> <gloss>carp fish</gloss> fried in clarified butter and prepared with fruit juices in goat meat broth, followed by drinking the remaining broth. 10
> Thus ends the formula for conception.

Prepare a paste of fish meat seasoned with asafoetida, rock salt, and coriander. Mix this with wheat flour and cook as cakes in clarified butter. Cook fish in buffalo meat broth until it is unctuous, sour, and salty. Once the broth is absorbed, mash the fish and add black pepper, cumin, coriander, a small amount of asafoetida, and fresh clarified butter. Use this as a filling for the black gram cakes. These two cake recipes are aphrodisiacs, strength-promoting, sources of joy and good fortune, nourishing, and supreme boosters of reproductive vitality. 11
> Thus ends the two aphrodisiac cake formulas.
